In this lesson, you will learn about a basic microwave communication system consisting of a transmitter and receiver.
INTRODUCTIONM
In basic terms, a communication system must have the ability to process, transmit, receive and interface information with a user.
You are already familiar with forms of communication such as radio, telephone and television.
Microwave communications operate on the same basic principles as the other forms of communication, only the frequencies, configurations and types of components are different.

BASIC MICROWAVE SYSTEMS
A microwave system is designed for the purpose of communicating a message or a group of messages.
Microwave Communication Systemmunication System
DISCUSSION
The messages to be communicated are defined as information or data.
This information or data could be in the form of voice, teletype, telemetry, video or any other form of coded intelligence.
The block diagram illustrates the major stages of a basic microwave communication system. Let's discuss each stage.
The input INFORMATION PROCESSOR functions to make the incoming information or data suitable for transmission.
The processing can be as simple as coupling the information to the next block. Or it can be as complex as coding or multiplexing the information.
The OSCILLATOR AND MODULATOR are responsible for developing the carrier frequency and for putting the information or data on the carrier.
The TRANSMITTER amplifies the modulated carrier for transmission. tters are covered in lesson 3.
The WAVEGUIDE acts like a conductor, routing the amplified modulated carrier to the antenna. aveguides act like conductors.
The TRANSMIT ANTENNA directs the microwave energy towards the receive antenna. Microwave antennas are covered in lesson 6.
The RECEIVE ANTENNA picks up the direct wave microwave signals.
The WAVEGUIDE routes the received signals to the receiver. Microwave receivers are covered in lesson 4.
The RECEIVER boosts the strength of the microwave energy received by the antenna to overcome losses due to noise or other atmospheric conditions.
Also, the modulated RF microwave signal is demodulated in the receiver.
The output INFORMATION PROCESSOR decodes or demultiplexes the data, if necessary, and outputs the data to the user.
As you have seen, a basic microwave communication system is very similar to an AM or FM radio communication system.

There are three major differences between microwave communications and lower frequency communication systems.
Let's discuss multi-channel operation, or multiplexing, first.
Multiplexing is a method that allows several messages to be transmitted on one carrier frequency.
Multiplexing was developed because the number of wires and radio frequency channels could not meet the demand for message transmission.
The operation is quite simple, even though the circuits are complex.
The multiplexer combines all incoming messages from users into one composite information signal.
The one composite information signal is then used to modulate the carrier signal for transmission.
At the receiver, the modulated carrier signal is demultiplexed, (the messages are separated).
Then each separate message is sent to the user..
There are several different methods used to multiplex information.
Repeater stations are required because microwave transmission is limited to line of sight. (Graphics Text)Multi-Channel Operation Repeater Stations Components and Devices
Recall that microwave propagation is direct wave.............
The range for microwave transmission is limited to approximately 25 to 50 miles due to the curvature of the earth.
For communications over longer distances, repeater stations are used.
Repeater stations are nothing more than a receiver and transmitter.
The transmitted signal from the original transmitter or from another repeater station is received by the repeater's receiver and fed to the repeater's transmitter.
The repeater's transmitter then transmits the signal to another repeater station or to the final destination.
Repeater stations are equipped with signal monitoring devices, but there is no signal processing or modulating equipment.
Also, in most cases, repeater stations are unattended.
The last major difference in microwave communication systems involves the components and devices used. ics Text)Multi-Channel Operation Repeater Stations Components and Devices
The high frequencies of the microwave region make it impractical for using ordinary components.

The following is a list of devices and/or components designed for microwave systems.
A klystron tube is a special type of vacuum tube. It is a source of microwave frequency energy. Klystrons also are used for amplifiers.
There are other types of tubes such as the magnetron and the traveling wave tube. Lesson 7 covers tube microwave generating devices in detail.
In the last few years, semiconductor microwave devices have been developed.
Devices such as the tunnel diode, PIN diode, varactor, microwave transistors and crystal detectors are replacing tube devices.
Waveguides act like conductors, passing microwave frequencies from one point to another.
Waveguides are manufactured in various shapes and sizes, and for special purposes. Terminators, bends, twists, connector tees, flanges, and rotary joints are some examples.
Waveguides are also used as tuners, impedance matching devices and attenuators.
The following are some of the special waveguides used in microwaves.
Dielectric Resonator Oscillator (DRO) is the unit that generates the microwave frequency. It receives external power and a modulation signal. M
The DRO outputs a modulated RF signal (10.5 GHz in the Model 330 Trainer) directly into the waveguide.
The VARIABLE ATTENUATOR provides a convenient means of adjusting the waveguide power level.
The attenuator consists of a slotted section of waveguide in which a matched resistive strip can be inserted to various depths.
The amount of attenuation or energy absorption is dependent on the depth of the strip penetration into the waveguide.
The CROSSGUIDE COUPLER is a section of waveguide with provisions for coupling two signals.
One signal is for measuring the transmitter frequency through a wavemeter or a crystal detector.
The other signal goes to a termination or dummy load, to prevent reflections on the waveguide system.
A SLIDE SCREW TUNER is used for matching waveguides to other components.
The tuner consists of a slotted section of waveguide on which is mounted an adjustable probe.
The position and penetration of the probe may be varied to introduce an impedance discontinuity to cancel out existing mismatches elsewhere.
Waveguide SLOTTED LINES are fundamental tools for the measurement of the magnitude and phase of standing waves (VSWR).
Such information may be transformed readily into impedance of the terminal load of the system or component.
The slotted line may also be used to measure percentage of transmitted or reflected power.
Its construction is similar to the slide screw tuner with a traveling probe carriage mounted on a slotted waveguide section.
In the slotted line, the probe is used for sampling the electric field along the slot to permit precise plotting of variations along the length of the slot.
The probe feeds a detector which produces a rectified output to operate a meter which indicates the relative voltage magnitude resulting in a standing wave pattern.
The measurement of the distance from minimum readings on the line is also used to determine frequency.
A CRYSTAL DETECTOR is the simplest and most sensitive microwave energy detector.
It consists of a silicon or germanium crystal placed in the microwave field. The crystal acts as a current generator.
When the microwave signal is applied across it, the rectified current output is proportional to the square of the applied voltage.
The RESONANT CAVITY WAVEMETER is the most commonly used microwave frequency measuring device.
It consists of a metal cylinder coupled to a waveguide. The cavity within the cylinder is resonant at one frequency by virtue of its volume.
The frequency of the cavity wavemeter is adjusted by varying the position of one of the end plates with a micrometer screw.
Thus, the micrometer reading at the point where loss occurs, resonance, will give the frequency of the energy in the waveguide.

The signal horn is the last item on the transmitter waveguide. It is the antenna used to direct or aim the radiated RF energy.
The receiver waveguide system uses the same type of antenna. This antenna picks up the transmitted signal and directs it down the waveguide.
The received signal is processed by the Down Converter and sent to PC130-308 where the information signal is separated from the carrier. The Down Converter is sealed like the DRO.
Experiment card PC130-308 contains the circuitry required to produce the IF frequency and separate the information signal from the carrier signal.

The signal horn is the last item on the transmitter waveguide. It is the antenna used to direct or aim the radiated RF energy.
The receiver waveguide system uses the same type of antenna. This antenna picks up the transmitted signal and directs it down the waveguide.
The received signal is processed by the Down Converter and sent to PC130-308 where the information signal is separated from the carrier. The Down Converter is sealed like the DRO.
Experiment card PC130-308 contains the circuitry required to produce the IF frequency and separate the information signal from the carrier signal.
In future experiments, you will investigate this circuit to learn how the IF signal is developed.
